node.label: Patricia Nelson Limerick
node.date_label: Desert Passages (1985) · The Legacy of Conquest (1987) · Trails, co-editor (1991) · Something in the Soil (2000)
node.description: In The Legacy of Conquest (1987), Patricia Nelson Limerick argued that the American West should be understood through conquest and its continuing consequences. Economic conflict and relationships among its peoples persist beyond the supposed closing of the frontier. Her co-edited Trails: Toward a New Western History (1991) helped articulate this turn toward an ongoing regional history. Alan Taylor’s “The Old Frontiers” (2008) praised her criticism of Turner’s exclusionary historical cast; Philip J. Deloria later credited her example as a writer. Her regional approach also drew criticism: reviewing All Over the Map (1996) in 1998, Thomas D. Isern found much of her essay familiar and questioned whether treating region as a setting advanced its conceptual understanding, while acknowledging that such advancement was not her purpose. Her work with Richard White on The Frontier in American Culture (1994) connected scholarship to a public exhibition about frontier imagery.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Desert Passages: Encounters with the American Deserts (1985); The Legacy of Conquest: The Unbroken Past of the American West (1987); Trails: Toward a New Western History (co-editor with Clyde A. Milner II and Charles E. Rankin, 1991); The Frontier in American Culture (with Richard White; edited by James R. Grossman, 1994); All Over the Map: Rethinking American Regions (with Edward L. Ayers, Stephen Nissenbaum and Peter S. Onuf, 1996); Something in the Soil: Legacies and Reckonings in the New West (2000); A Ditch in Time: The City, the West, and Water (2012).
node.scope_note: Monographs and Trails chapters are unread in full. Entry arguments use publisher and professional descriptions, Taylor’s named quotation, and Isern’s displayed review. Selected Cronon and Deloria passages were freshly read. The 1989 appraisal panel’s substantive text remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: As quoted and endorsed in Alan Taylor’s “The Old Frontiers” (2008), Limerick criticized Turner’s frontier account for centring English-speaking white men and marginalizing other historical participants.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of Taylor, “The Old Frontiers,” 7 May 2008, paragraph beginning “Turner’s sharpest” (web line 60), with preceding paragraphs 57–59. Taylor quotes Limerick’s charge of being “ethnocentric and nationalist.” This is a named-reader route. The quoted Limerick work is unspecified in Taylor’s paragraph and no original page or publication attribution is supplied. The Legacy of Conquest is unread; no rejection of every Turner proposition is asserted.
proposed_edges.map_label: Criticizes exclusions in the frontier thesis

proposed_edges.relationship: Limerick and White each contributed an essay to The Frontier in American Culture (1994), the companion volume to the Newberry Library exhibition, edited by James R. Grossman.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh JSTOR publisher record: author and editor credits, copyright 1994, description of Newberry exhibition; contents assign separate essays. This is joint book authorship with separate essay responsibility. Full essays unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Separate essays in one exhibition volume

proposed_edges.relationship: In “The Writer’s Studio with Philip J. Deloria” (2021), Deloria names Limerick among the scholars from whom he learned about writing and praises how her whimsical presence enters her prose.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh Cambridge HTML, question “Which scholars do you most admire as writers and why?”, answer first paragraph, web lines 506–508; issue pp. 305–313. Deloria says he “learned a lot” from Limerick, Cronon and White. The claim concerns prose, not supervision or the derivation of Playing Indian. No particular Limerick work is identified; none supplied. Selected professional-method passages read; later personal/family material is unused.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “A Place for Stories: Nature, History, and Narrative” (1992), Cronon credits Limerick’s remark as the source of his epigram about the material constraints on environmental storytelling.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh author-hosted journal scan, printed p. 1372, ecological-constraints paragraph and note 45; also p. 1347 acknowledgment. Note 45 says “a remark of Patricia Limerick’s”; it credits the immediately preceding dust epigram. The surrounding claim that stories must make ecological sense is Cronon’s formulation. No sole authorship of his narrative theory is inferred. Read p. 1347 and selected pp. 1371–1374; remainder not closely read. Running heads establish March 1992 despite the PDF filename’s 1991.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Legacy of Conquest (1987) brought environmental history into Limerick’s reinterpretation of the American West, as the MacArthur Foundation’s account of her scholarship explicitly recognizes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh MacArthur award biography, “About Patricia’s Work,” web line 54, explicitly lists “environmental history” and then discusses the book’s conquest framework. This mediated professional account supports inclusion in the field, not a fresh reading of the monograph or the claim that she founded environmental history.

proposed_edges.relationship: With White, Limerick contributed The Frontier in American Culture (1994) to the interpretation of frontier images through a Newberry Library exhibition and its companion book.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: JSTOR book description identifies the exhibition mounted in fall 1994 and its treatment of images, metaphors and reenactments, together with both author credits. “Public history” is the editorial field classification of this documented exhibition/book work. University biography corroborates her public-facing historical practice. Exhibition not visited and complete essays unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Interpreting frontier images for exhibition audiences

proposed_edges.relationship: As Lauck documents (2011), Woodward’s The Burden of Southern History (1960) provided a model for Limerick’s project that became The Legacy of Conquest (1987).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Lauck reconstructs the project from correspondence. This is a documented model, not inferred from seminar attendance. LSU Press supplies the corrected original year; neither book nor the letters were read directly.

proposed_edges.relationship: As Kearns reports (1998), Limerick criticized the frontier-process approach exemplified by Cronon, Miles and Gitlin’s “Becoming West” (1992) for privileging Anglo-American east-to-west movement over other populations’ movements.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mediated through Kearns’s substantive analysis; underlying chapter unread. He also reports Limerick’s later definitional truce (p. 398). This differs from the excluded epigram credit.

proposed_edges.relationship: In his opening contribution to ‘The Legacy of Conquest, by Patricia Nelson Limerick: A Panel of Appraisal’ (1989), Donald Worster assessed Limerick's The Legacy of Conquest (1987) as a candidate either to generate new research or to articulate an emerging trend in western history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher's linked Article PDF first page preview visually, including Worster's first two paragraphs, through the beginning of his summary at the bottom of p. 303. The quotation refers back to the two possible roles for a significant historical book set out in his first paragraph. The page also identifies the book's original publication as 1987. This records Worster's own evaluative prose. Only this first page of the 303–322 panel was read; later assessments and any criticisms remain unread. Accordingly this is an undirected review comparison, with no claim that Worster adopted Limerick's framework or that the book actually achieved the influence he considers possible.
